topic: The Definition of Workflow and the Kanban board

notes.front: What is a Definition of Workflow, in The Kanban Guide?
notes.back: The explicit shared understanding of flow among Kanban system members within their context.
notes.explanation: The Guide calls it a fundamental concept of Kanban: all its other elements depend heavily on how workflow is defined.
notes.example: A team agreeing, and writing down, what a unit of work is, when it counts as started and finished, and how it moves between.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: What does “DoW” stand for in The Kanban Guide?
notes.back: Definition of Workflow.
notes.explanation: The Guide uses the abbreviation throughout, including for the plural “DoWs”.
notes.example: “Our DoW says an item starts when someone moves it into Build.”
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: What is a work item, in The Kanban Guide?
notes.back: An individual unit of value moving through the workflow. The Guide also calls them items.
notes.explanation: Defining work items is the first of the DoW’s minimum elements: flow is measured in them.
notes.example: A customer request, a feature or a support ticket, whatever the team treats as one unit of value.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: What are started and finished points, in The Kanban Guide?
notes.back: The DoW’s definition of when work items count as started and when they count as finished within the workflow.
notes.explanation: They mark where the workflow begins and ends. The Guide’s measurements, taught later, use these same points.
notes.example: Started when an item is pulled into “Build”; finished when it reaches “Done”.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: What is a state, in a Definition of Workflow?
notes.back: A defined stage that work items flow through between started and finished.
notes.explanation: The DoW must have one or more of them, and its explicit policies say how items flow through each.
notes.example: “Build” and “Test” in a workflow that runs from “Build” to “Done”.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: What is WIP, in The Kanban Guide?
notes.back: Work in progress: any work items between a started point and a finished point.
notes.explanation: WIP depends on where the DoW puts started and finished: items before the start or past the finish are not WIP.
notes.example: Of six items on a board, one not yet started, three between started and finished, and two finished: WIP is three.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: What is WIP control, as a DoW element?
notes.back: The DoW’s definition of how WIP will be controlled from started to finished.
notes.explanation: The Guide requires the DoW to say how WIP is controlled but leaves the form of that control to the Kanban system members.
notes.example: “At most four items between Started and Finished” is one way of controlling WIP.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: What are explicit policies, as a DoW element?
notes.back: Stated rules about how work items can flow through each state from started to finished.
notes.explanation: Making the rules explicit means everyone works to the same understanding of how items move.
notes.example: “An item may enter Test only after a code review” is an explicit policy.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: What is Cycle Time, in The Kanban Guide?
notes.back: The elapsed time between when a work item started and when it finished.
notes.explanation: It is one of the Guide’s required measurements. The next card shows how it is used to set a service level expectation (SLE).
notes.example: An item started on Monday 3rd and finished on Thursday 6th has a Cycle Time of about three days of elapsed time.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Flow Metrics”, p. 7

notes.front: What is an SLE, in The Kanban Guide?
notes.back: A service level expectation: a forecast of how long it should take a work item to flow from started to finished.
notes.explanation: It is one of the DoW’s minimum elements, and it has two parts: a period of elapsed time and a probability.
notes.example: “85% of work items will be finished in eight days or less”, the Guide’s own example.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: What is a Kanban board?
notes.back: The visualization of the DoW.
notes.explanation: Showing at least the minimum DoW elements on the board lets everyone see what is happening, so they can run the workflow well and improve it.
notes.example: The board in the figure: states as columns, started and finished lines, work items, policies, a WIP control and the SLE.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 6

image.alt: An illustrative Kanban board with four columns: Ready (not started), Build, Test and Done. A dashed STARTED line separates Ready from Build and a dashed FINISHED line separates Test from Done. Six cards (Item A to F) sit in the columns, three of them between the lines. Build carries the note ‘Policy: done when reviewed’ and Test ‘Policy: done when tests pass’. Below: ‘WIP control: at most 4 items between STARTED and FINISHED (WIP now: 3)’ and ‘SLE: 85% of items finish in 8 days or less’. A footnote says the layout is illustrative and the Guide sets no required layout.
image.credit: Drawn for this deck from The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, pp. 5–6

notes.front: According to the Guide, what depends heavily on how workflow is defined?
notes.back: All the other elements of the Guide.
notes.explanation: That is why the Guide calls the DoW a fundamental concept of Kanban.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: Must Kanban system members use every one of the Guide’s minimum elements when creating their DoW?
notes.back: Yes. At a minimum, they must create their DoW using all of the listed elements.
notes.explanation: The elements are a floor, not a menu: members may add more but may not leave any out.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: How many minimum elements of a DoW does the Guide list?
notes.back: Six: work items, started and finished points, states, WIP control, explicit policies and an SLE.
notes.explanation: The Guide lists them as six bullets without stating the number.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: Can a workflow have more than one started point or finished point?
notes.back: Yes. Depending on the work item, a workflow may have more than one started or finished point.
notes.explanation: The Guide requires a definition of when items start and finish, not a single fixed line.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: How many defined states must a DoW have between started and finished?
notes.back: One or more.
notes.explanation: Even a single state between the started and finished points meets the Guide’s minimum.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: Over what span of the workflow must the DoW define how WIP is controlled?
notes.back: From started to finished.
notes.explanation: The same span that defines WIP itself: everything between a started point and a finished point.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: What must a DoW’s explicit policies be about?
notes.back: How work items can flow through each state from started to finished.
notes.explanation: Rules for each state, so nobody has to guess how an item moves on.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: What are the two parts of an SLE?
notes.back: A period of elapsed time, and a probability associated with that period.
notes.explanation: For example, “85% of work items will be finished in eight days or less”: eight days is the time, 85% the probability.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: Does the Guide require an SLE of “85% within eight days”?
notes.back: No. That is only the Guide’s example. Each SLE should be based on its own past Cycle Times, or a best guess until they exist.
notes.explanation: The Guide says the SLE should be based on historical Cycle Time.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: What should an SLE be based on?
notes.back: Historical Cycle Time.
notes.explanation: The SLE forecasts how long items should take, so it is grounded in how long past items actually took.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: Once an SLE has been calculated, where should it be visualized?
notes.back: On the DoW (the Guide’s words). In practice, wherever the DoW is shown, such as the Kanban board.
notes.explanation: It is one of the DoW’s minimum elements, so it belongs with the others where everyone can see it.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: Does the Guide set an order in which the DoW’s minimum elements must be put in place?
notes.back: No. The order is not important, as long as all of them are adopted.
notes.explanation: What matters is that every minimum element ends up in the DoW.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: Besides the minimum elements, what does the Guide say Kanban system members often add to a DoW?
notes.back: Elements such as values, principles and working agreements, depending on their circumstances.
notes.explanation: The Guide says the options vary and points to resources beyond itself for choosing them.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: Does the Guide set a minimum or maximum number of DoWs?
notes.back: No. It encourages a DoW wherever Kanban system members need to connect flow to value realization.
notes.explanation: Members often need more than one, for example for different groups or different levels of the organization.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: What does the Guide say it is essential to make transparent on a Kanban board?
notes.back: At least the minimum elements of the DoW.
notes.explanation: The Guide says this is essential: it gives the team the information it needs to run and keep improving the workflow.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: Does the Guide prescribe how a Kanban board should look?
notes.back: No. There are no specific guidelines; Kanban system members are limited only by their imagination.
notes.explanation: The Guide asks only that the minimum DoW elements be transparent and that all aspects of the DoW and context be considered.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: What does the Guide say should be considered when designing a visualization of the DoW?
notes.back: All aspects of the DoW, such as work items and policies, plus other context-specific factors that may affect how value flows.
notes.explanation: No layout is required, but the design should reflect the whole DoW and the context.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: Must a Kanban board show states as columns?
notes.back: No. The Kanban Pocket Guide notes that nothing requires columns for states; circles or spirals would do.
notes.explanation: This follows from the Guide’s “no specific guidelines” for how a visualization should look.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 4 “The Kanban Board”, PDF p. 53
notes.sourceLicence: C · all rights reserved (facts only, our wording)

notes.front: Is To Do → Doing → Done, with Doing as started and Done as finished, a valid Kanban workflow?
notes.back: Yes. The Kanban Pocket Guide calls it perfectly valid: it has one state between started and finished.
notes.explanation: The Guide’s minimum is one or more defined states between started and finished.
notes.source: The Kanban Pocket Guide (Vacanti, Singh and Johnson, 2022), ch. 4 “Workflow States”, PDF p. 49
notes.sourceLicence: C · all rights reserved (facts only, our wording)

notes.front: Two members disagree on whether an item has started when it is assigned or when work on it begins. What should settle this, according to the Guide?
notes.back: The DoW: the team’s explicit shared definition of when work items are started and finished.
notes.explanation: The DoW exists to give members an explicit shared understanding of flow; without it, metrics and decisions rest on guesses.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: A team decides that each customer request is one unit of value moving through its workflow. Which DoW element has it defined?
notes.back: Its work items.
notes.explanation: The first minimum element is a definition of the individual units of value moving through the workflow.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: A team counts an item finished when it is released, but for urgent fixes when a hotfix is applied. Does this break the Guide’s rules?
notes.back: No. Depending on the work item, a workflow may have more than one finished point, as long as each is defined.
notes.explanation: The Guide requires a definition for when items are started and finished, and allows more than one of each.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: An item sits in a “Ready” list before the team’s started point. Is it WIP?
notes.back: No. Only work items between a started point and a finished point are WIP.
notes.explanation: Before the started point, the item has not yet entered the part of the workflow WIP counts.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: An item is in “Test”, after the started point and before the finished point. Is it WIP?
notes.back: Yes. Any work item between a started point and a finished point is WIP.
notes.explanation: It has started and not yet finished, whatever state it is in.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: A team’s DoW defines its work items, states, started and finished points, policies and SLE, but says nothing on how many items may be in progress. What is missing?
notes.back: WIP control: a definition of how WIP will be controlled from started to finished.
notes.explanation: All six minimum elements must be adopted; this DoW has five.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: A team’s DoW defines a started point and a finished point but no states between them. Does it meet the Guide’s minimum?
notes.back: No. The DoW needs one or more defined states that work items flow through from started to finished.
notes.explanation: Defined states are one of the six minimum elements, and all must be adopted.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: A note on the board reads: “An item may enter Test only after a code review.” Which DoW element is this?
notes.back: An explicit policy.
notes.explanation: It states how work items can flow from one state to the next.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: A team writes its SLE as “Items finish in 10 days or less.” Is that a complete SLE?
notes.back: No. It has the elapsed time but no probability, such as “85% of items”.
notes.explanation: An SLE has two parts: a period of elapsed time and a probability associated with it.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: A brand-new team has no Cycle Time data yet. Can it have an SLE?
notes.back: Yes. A best guess will do until there is enough historical data for a proper SLE calculation.
notes.explanation: The SLE should be based on historical Cycle Time, but the Guide allows a best guess while there is none.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: A manager tells the team its SLE is a deadline it must hit for every item. What does the Guide call an SLE?
notes.back: A forecast of how long a work item should take from started to finished, not a deadline.
notes.explanation: ProKanban’s own FAQ likewise says an SLE is a forecast rather than a target.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5; ProKanban.org, /kpg FAQ
notes.sourceLicence: B · CC BY-SA 4.0 (Guide); C · © 2026 ProKanban.org, all rights reserved; facts only, in our own words (FAQ)

notes.front: A team defines its states and policies this week and adds its WIP control next week. Has it broken the Guide’s rules?
notes.back: No. The order of adopting the DoW elements is not important, as long as all are adopted.
notes.explanation: The Guide requires every minimum element but sets no sequence.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: Three teams each have a DoW, and their department wants a fourth DoW for the flow of larger initiatives across teams. Does the Guide allow this?
notes.back: Yes. Multiple DoWs can serve different groups or levels of the organization; the Guide sets no maximum.
notes.explanation: It encourages a DoW wherever members need to connect flow to value realization.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: A team adds a working agreement, “We all help on anything blocked for a day”, to its DoW. Is that allowed?
notes.back: Yes. The Guide says members often need additional DoW elements, such as working agreements.
notes.explanation: The minimum elements are a floor; values, principles and working agreements can be added.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: This board shows work items, started and finished points, states, policies and a WIP control. Which minimum DoW element is missing?
notes.back: The SLE.
notes.explanation: The Guide says the SLE should be visualized on the DoW, and at least the minimum elements must be transparent on the board.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 6

No service level expectation is shown.

notes.front: A team wants its board drawn as a circle, with states as segments, not columns. Does the Guide allow it?
notes.back: Yes. There are no specific guidelines for how a visualization should look, provided the minimum DoW elements are transparent.
notes.explanation: Members are limited only by their imagination in how they make flow transparent.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: What is the difference between the DoW and the Kanban board?
notes.back: The DoW is the members’ explicit shared understanding of flow; the Kanban board is the visualization of it.
notes.explanation: Change the DoW and the board should change with it; the board alone is not the definition.
notes.contrast: Definition versus picture of the definition.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 6

notes.front: What is the difference between WIP and WIP control?
notes.back: WIP is the work items between started and finished. WIP control is the DoW’s definition of how their number is controlled.
notes.explanation: One is what is in progress; the other is the rule that keeps it in check.
notes.contrast: WIP is a quantity; WIP control is a policy about that quantity.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5

notes.front: What is the difference between Cycle Time and an SLE?
notes.back: Cycle Time is how long a finished item actually took. An SLE forecasts, from past Cycle Times, how long items should take.
notes.explanation: The SLE looks forward and carries a probability; Cycle Time is a measurement of what already happened.
notes.source: The Kanban Guide (May 2025), “Defining and Visualizing the Workflow”, p. 5
